content: Lymphadenopathy, derived from the Greek words adenas (meaning gland) and patheia (meaning act of suffering or disease), refers to lymph nodes that are abnormal in size, number, or consistency. It is often used interchangeably with the terms swollen or enlarged lymph nodes. The most common causes of lymphadenopathy include infections, autoimmune diseases, and malignancies. Lymphadenopathy can be classified into subtypes or groups based on specific characteristics. Other variants of lymphadenopathy may also exist, but these are not detailed here. The pathophysiology of lymphadenopathy involves specific mechanisms of disease development. Certain genetic mutations or alterations in specific genes have been associated with the development of lymphadenopathy, often involving particular molecular pathways. On gross pathological examination, certain findings are characteristic of lymphadenopathy. Similarly, microscopic histopathological analysis reveals distinct features that are diagnostic of the condition. Lymphadenopathy may be caused by a variety of factors, including infections, autoimmune processes, or malignancies. In some cases, it is linked to specific genetic mutations in particular genes. However, there are instances where no established cause can be identified. It is essential to differentiate lymphadenopathy from other diseases that may present with similar findings, such as other conditions causing lymph node enlargement or swelling. Common risk factors for the development of lymphadenopathy include underlying infections, immune dysregulation, or genetic predispositions. The diagnosis of lymphadenopathy is made based on specific diagnostic criteria. These criteria must be met to confirm the presence of the condition. Lymphadenopathy is often asymptomatic, meaning that affected individuals may not experience noticeable symptoms.
